However, run your boost all the way down to zero and your default speed will be strangled momentarily as your engine coughs back to life. Versatile racers have a drift bar that’s consumed in chunks, meaning you can’t stop a boost once you’ve started. It means they’re not a great fit for navigating the urban, grid-like portions of the maps, because it can be hard to force them into the right direction when in the middle of a briefly unstoppable boost.

Drifters are my preferred class, since they’re the easiest to sling sideways and therefore the best fit for an arcade racing game. The other classes are less satisfying to drift, and there sometimes seems as if there’s even a bit of a speed penalty for doing so. There were definitely occasions it was overtly faster to Hail Melon around a corner, Ross Chastain-style, than it was to slide into it properly. This shouldn’t really be the case in any arcade racer.

The biggest problem with Infinite Rush is how surprisingly generic the open-world approach makes it feel. It doesn’t have a single, large open map to explore like, say, Burnout Paradise or Forza Horizon 6. Instead, there are four separate, modestly sized islands – each themed in slightly different ways. There’s Wheelswood, a commercial-style, downtown-inspired map; Tentacle Bay, another city-oriented environment, only with a little more open countryside; Gearville, a desert-themed, industrial zone; and Drifty Temples, an East Asian-inspired island. I just find myself blazing through them, smashing through bushes and benches. There’s some decent imagination on display – and I do think the huge Hot Wheels Mount Rushmore on Gearville is pretty cute – but broadly speaking there’s just not much that grabs my attention. Not even the big, plastic animals.

In the Unleashed games, you find yourself racing through half-built skyscrapers above the clouds – or staring up at enormous arcade cabinets, which might as well be skyscrapers themselves with the way they loom over your tiny toy cars, from down on the sticky carpet. Infinite Rush has absolutely none of this scale, and it’s all the worse for it. They’re not quite believable dioramas, even if they’re filled with moulded plastic props. But they’re not quite real places either – even if the default measure of distance to my next waypoint is metres. 800 metres away, in a car that’s ostensibly three inches long? Something’s not adding up.

In a word, these maps are bland. You just drive back and forth across them, competing in a genre-typical range of event types. The racing is still fine, although the tracks are nowhere near as interesting anymore because they simply can’t use their surroundings in the same way as the Unleashed games can. There you can race on the floors, across the furniture, up in the air vents – you name it. Infinite Rush has none of that. Worse, a lot of the side activities that appear to be here to justify these open-world maps are just busywork – like photograph challenges that tell you exactly where to take them, or checkpoint collections that’d be a lot less trivial to complete if you actually had to dodge traffic (which you don’t; smashing through them doesn’t even really slow you down).

[In the Unleashed games] you can race on the floors, across the furniture, up in the air vents – you name it. Infinite Rush has none of that.

There was probably a way to experiment and take the series to an open world without sacrificing the sense of scale Unleashed got so right. Could the desert map have been built on a beach, or one of the other maps laid out in the foyer of a toy store? Anything like this would’ve given the backdrops the scale Infinite Rush lacks. Could more of the architecture have been household objects, with cereal box buildings standing side by side with Hot Wheels garage playsets, and painted roads filling the gaps between the iconic orange track pieces? I just feel like there was a more imaginative way to tackle this shift. 2023’s LEGO 2K Drive did this approach better overall, but unfortunately that game is already completely delisted in digital stores.

The profound shift in map philosophy is doubly disappointing considering the improvements Infinite Rush makes elsewhere. For instance, it now comes with four-player splitscreen, which would’ve been amazing fun in the massively more imaginative Unleashed maps. It also now features the ability for AI to race on your custom tracks, which would’ve been another huge boost to longevity for the older games. I would’ve loved to have seen how the AI handled the wild leaps of the crazy routes I’ve created in the past (especially since Infinite Rush is way, way more restrictive in terms of the height limit than the Unleashed games – which feature multi-level maps with a ton of vertical space). Infinite Rush also features the new ability to change out wheels as part of the customisation suite, which speaks to me as a 40-odd-year-old diorama-building dork who loves swapping out wheels on his Hot Wheels cars. Okay, they’re not always mine, but my boys aren’t using them anymore; just don’t tell them I’ve been attacking their collection with a power drill.

items.title: Stranger Things: Tales From ’85 Season 2 Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
Stranger Things: Tales From ’85, Netflix’s animated series spin-off of their Stranger Things live-action series, returns for a Valentine’s Day-themed season set in early February 1985. After , Nikki Baxter (Odessa A’zion) is now a full-fledged member of Dustin’s (Braxton Quinney) Hawkins Investigators Club or HIC. He remains the ever-enthusiastic adventurer dedicated to their club even though nightly group hunts for the weird and supernatural have unearthed nothing. But Hawkins doesn’t stay quiet for long — a petty robbery at the Palace Arcade coincides with the disappearance of town delinquent Charlie Dandridge (Benjamin Valic) and a field of ominous bioluminescent flowers popping up in the woods.

Intrigued, the HIC quickly discover that the flowers are actually Audrey II-looking critters being harvested by glowing blue “hate sprites,” as dubbed by Max, and they’re friendly. In fact, they’re harbingers of a bigger ghost-like creature that’s on the hunt for humans. Across the eight episodes of this season, the kids will determine why they’ve shown up, how they tie into the lore of Hawkins’ founding, and deal with some other unfinished business from last season.

On the character front, the impending romantic holiday brings out the worst in Max (Jolie Hoang-Rappaport), who picks plenty of fights with Lucas (Elisha “EJ” Williams), which ties into their canon on again/off again status referred to in Season 3 of the live-action series. Eleven (Brooklyn Davey Norstedt) and Mike (Luca Diaz) also continue to figure out what they are, even though Eleven remains as fiercely protective of Mike as ever.

Stranger Things: Tales From ’85 Season 2 is more focused on the core crew of characters and integrates Nikki nicely into the friend dynamic. Parents don’t factor into their late-night roamings, and even Steve Harrington is MIA. While the new mystery involves some unknown town history and an important character from Season 1, overall the scripts continue to pale in comparison to the live-action series. Characterization is kept simple, with problems stemming from one-note issues like financial troubles in Nikki’s household or Max being upset with her absent father. Instead of trying — or being allowed — to fill in the blanks with this ensemble, the majority of the season is just interested in moving the plot along or setting up big action beats. While an animated series is usually the medium for big ideas to be brought to life, this second season is an example of “more is more.” It’s actually a bit exhausting to watch fight after fight and chase upon chase when we know the core kids are safe from anything serious happening to them because of where these stories live in the timeline.

Season 2 makes it more clear than ever that a season-long mystery of even a truncated eight episodes feels too long. The set pieces remain frustratingly winnable and repetitive, while the characters only advance in minuscule ways. In truth, Stranger Things: Tales From ’85 might have been better conceived as a “case of the week” series à la Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!, where each episode was more focused on the kids pairing up for individualized creative mysteries tailored to the tone and personalities of the characters. Unfortunately, this current format is not meeting the high writing standards of the Stranger Things franchise.

Stranger Things: Tales From ’85 Season 2 isn’t so much a sophomore slump as it is a status quo continuation of the good and the less-than-great from Season 1.

Where it excel is in the quality of its animation. Flying Bark Productions executes some very cool creatures this season with the sprites, ethereal bugs, and a “Big Bad” that is striking to see in action. The animated performances of each of the cast members also remain strong and in keeping with their live-action counterparts. Jolie Hoang-Rappaport as Max and Braxton Quinney as Dustin remain the vocal MVPs, adding a lot of energy to the season even when the story gets stuck in ruts or unnecessary side missions.

Stranger Things: Tales From ’85 Season 2 isn’t so much a sophomore slump as it is a status quo continuation of the good and the less-than-great from Season 1. This season’s mystery is a little more interesting, but it doesn’t have the kind of emotional weight or originality in story we expect from this franchise.

items.title: Slow Horses Season 6, Episode 1 Review — 'Circle of Life'
items.author: Leanne Butkovic
items.content:
This review contains full spoilers for Season 6, Episode 1, which is streaming on Apple TV now.

It’s the return of Slow Horses (along with a )! The questions looming over this new six-episode season were how well it would fare after losing its creator and head writer, Will Smith, while tackling two of Mick Herron’s Slough House novels instead of one. So far, Slow Horses seems the same as ever, even if it’s maybe trying a little too hard to prove that it knows how the show’s schtick is supposed to go. Even so, it’s hard to be too nitpicky with a series that cranks out new seasons like clockwork and reliably hits its marks.

“Circle of Life” sets up the chessboard of this season’s central mystery, which sees the Slow Horses being targeted. Someone’s picking off the flunky MI5 spies from Slough House; two former agents — who both seemed to be living quiet, unglamorous lives after the service — have been killed by an unidentified twosome (played by Andor’s Kyle Soller and The Witcher’s MyAnna Buring). The current roster also seems to have been entirely wiped from the Park’s systems, and their paychecks have stopped coming too. In protest, the greasy Jackson Lamb (Gary Oldman) goes on “strike,” which mostly means departing to the Italian restaurant below Slough House and uncorking a bottle of red wine before noon.

Diana Taverner (Kristin Scott Thomas), now comfortably First Chair after outsting the bumbling Claude Whelan at the end of Season 5, seems to have had a hand in Slough House’s expungement, though isn’t cleanly admitting to anything. Among all of this early drama, River Cartwright (Jack Lowden, maybe soon to graduate from shoddy spy to good spy) is grappling with — rather, trying to completely smother — the grief from the off-camera death of his struggling grandpa, David (Jonathan Pryce), as he plans the funeral.

The disturbing opening shot of Season 6 is a statement as much as it is a metaphor for the disregard of some lives: Slow Horses, now written by the show’s longtime co-executive producer Gaby Chiappe, is still . Chiappe might not have the same comedy writing background as Smith (who worked on shows like The Thick of It and Veep) that gave the show a certain edge, but Slow Horses still . Jackson Lamb still day-drinks and burps loudly (juxtaposed against one of the series’ most sentimental scenes showing River and David’s final moments together) and laughs at funerals (to his credit, it funny watching River eulogize about his grandpa’s deep care for the nation’s train systems as a coverup for his espionage work). Figured as much!

That’s not to say deploying the well-established character traits of each of Slow Horse’s fantastic ensemble is sloppy lever-pulling. For instance, it will basically always be funny when Roddy Ho (Christopher Chung) acts like… well, Roddy Ho. (Also, I’m 99.8% sure that was Ghost of Tsushima he was playing at work.) But I do sort of wish the series was a little more confident off the bat in trusting itself to tell the story it needs to tell with its characters responding as the ridiculous people they are without winking at the audience.

Already, Slow Horses has a lot of balls to juggle, but that’s nothing new. As arguably the most consistent spy series on TV right now, it’s always threaded complex storylines that opt for the less-obvious twist. It’s safe to expect that pretty much everything is a clue right now — What’s the connection between the seemingly irrelevant (for now) raid on the Russian finance botfarm, the spy-killers, River’s father Frank Harkness (Hugo Weaving), and the secret money that the slimy politician Peter Judd (Samuel West) funneled to Diana? — but I don’t expect any of them to piece together as nicely as they’d seem at first glance. But with only five episodes remaining, covering two books’ worth of material, Slow Horses has a lot of ground to cover — like, when are we seeing you-know-who again? — and not much time to do it.

items.title: DNX #1 Review: Marvel's X-Men/Fantastic Four Crossover Is Off to a Bland Start
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
Try as I might, I've had a very difficult time connecting with Marvel's current lineup of X-Men comics. At first, that sense of disconnect could be chalked up to the sting of losing the Krakoa status quo back in 2024. The Age of Krakoa was easily the most creatively fruitful period in the X-Men franchise since the heyday of Chris Claremont's run, and Marvel made a grave error in opting to wipe the slate clean rather than finding a way to move forward with the resilient mutant nation as the permanent baseline. But that apathy to the post-Krakoa X-Men line hasn't faded over the past two years. The X-Men franchise is stuck in a creative rut, and any hope that the DNX crossover will shake things loose is sadly dashed in the first issue.

DNX is ostensibly an X-Men/Fantastic Four crossover event, though its roots lie mainly in writer Jed MacKay's ongoing X-Men series and last year's Age of Revelation crossover. The premise behind the series is that both Cyclops and White Beast (the original, corrupted version of Hank McCoy who now leads the supervillain cabal known as 3K) have seen the future where a devastating virus has transformed humanity into mutants. Cyclops seeks to prevent that future from coming to pass, while White Beast wants to own that future. And now the simmering conflict between the X-Men and 3K comes to a head.

Frankly, I wish this issue were as efficient in laying out the scope of the conflict. But instead, the script gets very bogged down by exposition right from the get-go. There's too much emphasis on Cyclops explaining the stakes and summarizing recent X-events and not nearly enough on diving into the actual conflict. The result is that the story barely feels like it's gotten started by the time issue #1 reaches its end. With Marvel already in the midst of multiple other crossover events at the moment (Avengers: Armageddon and Queen in Black), DNX really needed to make a stronger case for itself starting out.

It doesn't help that the FF characters feel so superfluous here. They enter the story via a subplot involving regular Beast turning to Mister Fantastic to cure Magneto of his ongoing genetic malady. Even with that storytelling vector, it never feels like the Fantastic Four have a logical or organic reason for being a part of this conflict. This reads more like a regular arc of MacKay's X-Men run with an outside super-team shoehorned in. 2012's Age of Ultron showed there is potential in exploring the unlikely partnership between mutants and the Richards family (in the case, the Wolverine/Invisible Woman alliance), so hopefully DNX will eventually find some interesting veins to mine there.

DNX #1 only really works when it focuses on the 3K characters. Any team that forces characters like Cassandra Nova and Magneto's clone Joseph to work to work together is bound to be a flimsy arrangement at best, and McKay makes the most of that here. You almost have to feel sorry for White Beast as he sees his back-stabbing, deceitful allies snatching defeat from the jaws of victory and tries to hold the entire enterprise together through sheer force of will.

Artist Federico Vicentini and colorist David Curiel do their best to spice up what is a very dialogue-heavy first issue. Vicetini's figure work is inconsistent at best, particularly when it comes to character faces, but he does bring a palpable energy to the page that helps offset the plodding script. Maybe that comes at the expense of a few too many Dutch angle panels, but so be it. And Curiel's colors give everything a vivid look and feel, with some of the standout pages including a visual flashback to the Fatal Attractions crossover and the psyhcic battle between Quentin Quire and Cassandra Nova.

items.title: Resident Evil Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
Whatever your idea of what a good Resident Evil movie be, I have to recommend to the skeptical to put that to one side and lock in for what Zach Cregger delivers with this new adaptation of the Capcom games. With a clear appreciation for odds stacked against the protagonist and all manner of freaky foes to stand against them, Cregger ably adapts the spirit, if not the letter, of the Resident Evil games into a jet-fueled horror experience that has room for lots of tension, some great laughs, and a strong central performance from Austin Abrams.

What’s clear about Resident Evil from the first frame is that it’s got some serious pep in its step. At 95 minutes, Resident Evil is here for a good time, not a long time, and it hits the ground running as Bryan (Austin Abrams), a medical courier, accepts a last-minute assignment to bring a high-priority delivery through the mountains to Raccoon City General Hospital. We encounter our first zombie less than 10 minutes past that point, and from there, Cregger doesn’t ever let too long go by without putting Bryan through some funhouse maze of grotesquery he’s ill-equipped to contend with, and to frequently hilarious effect.

Yes, Resident Evil is often very funny, but never in a way that feels at the franchise’s expense. Cregger is broadly successful in judging how and when to lean into the campy nature of Resident Evil’s pedigree for comedic effect, or to what degree Bryan’s ineptitude should detour the action into a less predictable direction. Cregger is adept at building tension in a way that makes it impossible to get a read on if that tension will pay off in a laugh or a scare, and that unpredictable energy permeates Resident Evil. This dark comedic streak is a signature of Cregger’s at this point, and it’s a surprising and effective counterbalance to the world-shaking ramifications of the Raccoon City incident currently underway. Ironically, it’s only the handful of Resident Evil’s meta jokes about its video game heritage that ring a little hollow and dated; other than that, Cregger is largely very successful at understanding how to adapt a video game into a movie in a way that serves both mediums well, even when that means subverting expectations.

And as far as heroes go, Austin Abrams’ Bryan is definitely one for subverting expectations. Far from the Leon Kennedy or Chris Redfield action-hero mold, Bryan is an everyman just trying to make a bit of extra cash and navigate some high-stakes relationship issues with his offscreen girlfriend Michelle. After his scene-stealing turn in , Abrams easily shoulders his promotion to leading man here in a performance that’s a lot more skillful than the simplicity of the character first suggests. Abrams spends long stretches of Resident Evil as the only (human) actor onscreen, and Cregger pushes him into numerous scenarios where Bryan has to narrate his way through what he’s doing, often while also delivering on a comedic beat at the same time. The actor takes the frenetic energy of his Weapons character (he was the drug addict burglar in that movie) and focuses it down into something just as nervy, but a lot more grounded and relatable.

Yes, Bryan reacts like a normal human probably should when faced with tentacle monsters exploding out of places they shouldn’t, and Abrams and Cregger both really seem to delight in the character’s frequent overwhelm. It’s played for laughs most of the time, but that tendency towards being overwhelmed also forms the backbone of what simple character arc there is for Bryan to reckon with in the aftermath of his conversations with Michelle. Resident Evil makes no secret about what Bryan is struggling to wrap his head around, even as everyone around him devolves into snarling monsters, and though the movie doesn’t go very far out of its way to land any of that with any real weight, Bryan’s anxieties are serviceable enough to give structure and add some dimension to a few of the later encounters he has to survive.

With a tendency towards celebrating the feel of the games and not the specifics of the plot, Resident Evil succeeds in amplifying classic gameplay moments into horror movie beats in a way that goes far beyond simple fan service.

It’s a good thing that Abrams is as watchable as he is, because no member of Resident Evil’s supporting cast gets much more to do than drop in for a scene or two’s worth of exposition. No one’s bad acting-wise, there’s just very little room for anyone in the supporting cast to be really good. Paul Walter Hauser’s Umbrella Corporation functionary has just enough time in the spotlight to illustrate how terrible the Umbrella Corporation is, but characters like these are the trees on the side of the road that Resident Evil is racing by as it moves from beat to beat. As long as you’re having a good time with Abrams behind the wheel, this won’t matter at all, but if you’re on the fence, you may find yourself wishing you’d gotten some more time with some of Raccoon City’s citizenry.

Of course, the stars here are the poor, unfortunate souls afflicted by the t-Virus, which has a habit of rapidly mutating any human tissue it comes into contact with. There are some zombies here and there, but they’re as disposable to the experience of watching Resident Evil as they are to playing any Resident Evil game. It’s the more creative, nightmarish mutants which have evolved past “vanilla zombie” that really keep Resident Evil moving. By the time Cregger has trotted out just the film’s second infected creature, it’s clear that nothing breathing can be trusted not to erupt in a mess of whipping appendages and eyeballs, and more movies could use that kind of uncertainty as a ticking time bomb to take advantage of.

These creatures, which feel right at home with Resident Evil’s Lovecraftian design language, are all lovingly rendered by Cregger and his team, who luxuriate in their oozing, thrashing, slithering glory. Abrams’ big, shrieking reactions to these horrors feels more and more appropriate as the movie goes because they get increasingly disturbing (and blissfully, most of the good stuff has been held back from the marketing). Bryan’s journey to the heart of Raccoon City really becomes an excuse to tour as much of this genetic hellscape as possible, which means that the cycle of “new location, new gross monster to sidestep” may get tiresome, but the creativity of how Cregger introduces and then heightens these things often feels like it outpaces the rinse and repeat nature of how we discover them as we go.

With an obvious tendency towards celebrating the feel of the games and not the specifics of the plot, Resident Evil consistently succeeds in amplifying classic gameplay moments from the franchise into horror movie beats in a way that goes far beyond simple fan service and “I understood that reference” references. Searching for ammo, spotting an oncoming enemy, reloading on a time crunch as they close distance, getting a perfectly timed shot off, being lured into the dark by something you may not be equipped to deal with… Cregger’s Resident Evil is littered with touches like these that are actually used to ratchet up moment-to-moment dread and not just to pay lip service to gamers.

That carries through into Dariusz Wolski’s cinematography, which emphasizes Bryan’s perspective throughout and frequently emulates the third-person approach of the games in a way that heightens the terror of what we may find around the next corner. Wolski also plays with different light sources really well throughout Resident Evil, especially in an early scene where both the exterior and interior lights of a car are used to moody and tense effect as things go wrong on a snow-driven road. Co-composers Ryan and Hays Holladay also support Cregger’s efforts with a discordant, playful score that finds a good balance between boldly accentuating big moments and keeping tension simmering on the burner as Bryan stumbles his way through dark, new spaces.

items.title: Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave Review
items.author: Brendan Graeber
items.content:
The Fire Emblem series has always prided itself on how it teaches you to become a master tactician on the battlefield, using its turn-based battle system to push you to truly think strategically. In its more recent games, strategy became an important aspect not just while waging war, but between battles as well: How will you make the most of your time before the next skirmish? Who needs extra training, or perhaps a nice shared meal to increase camaraderie? Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave doesn’t just take the next step down that path, it makes an ambitious leap forward. It expands the scope of how you manage your budding heroes and explore its unexpectedly engaging map, and introduces some of the most harrowing and clever battles I’ve seen in the series to date. Its branching story intertwines into a grand epic that always seemed to have a new twist up its sleeve, and even after a hundred hours, I’ve still got more unique paths to tread that I’m itching to dive back into. Like a gladiator risking it all, Fortune’s Weave never stops aiming for the top – and it rarely misses that mark.

This story begins with an undead apocalypse already in progress, but while your customizable character is asked to stop it, you’ll soon learn that salvation is only to be found in the past. Thanks to some very on-brand time travel shenanigans, you must go back and ensure four legendary heroes survive the trials and tribulations that surround a series of colosseum matches known as the Heroic Games, each with their own path full of distinct, large-scale battles. 2019’s Fire Emblem: Three Houses similarly let you choose your own story path, but its first act played out largely the same before the second diverged depending on your faction choice. Fortune’s Weave not only flips that structure on its head, it also manages to make its finale more robust and impactful depending on how much of its main cast you reach the last act with.

This works thanks in large part to a single save file system that helps funnel each path toward one merged conclusion. I’ll admit that I had my reservations at first, as just one save slot initially seemed to limit replayability. However, Fortune’s Weave has a surprisingly good solution for managing these multiple paths. A nifty little hub room allows you to not only pick which story path you want to progress at almost any time, but even go back and replay any chapter you’ve done, no matter which act it’s in. Looking back will give you a snapshot of the army you had at the beginning of that chapter, who you’d recruited, and how strong they were – and if you choose to redo it, the snapshot for the following chapter will update with any differences, allowing you to keep progressing along this new playthrough without wiping data from any subsequent chapters further down the line that you’d already completed. It’s a smart way to weave the time travel theme into a mechanic that would be invaluable regardless, and lets you see nearly everything Fortune’s Weave has to offer without having to start from scratch on a new playthrough.

Each story path is wonderfully unique, offering different glimpses of life in the Dagdan Empire: Cai, the exuberant country kid in over his head as he tries to find a way to rescue his father from execution; Dietrich, the detached (and slightly unhinged) swordsman from a distant land who really only cares about finding worthy opponents for his blade; Theodora, queen of a southern kingdom seeking relief and acceptance for her people; and Leda, a talented musician and dancer on a quest for revenge against her father’s murderers. Each has an intriguing tale to tell as their personal quests lead them to the empire’s sprawling capital, Dagsion (imagine Rome if it was literally ruled over by the pantheon of gods), and I loved discovering the larger conspiracy lurking beneath it all as their journeys start to intertwine.

I admire how each story path is its own strand on a larger web of intrigue.

These four heroes are initially out to win the grand Heroic Games and win their heart's desire, but I was delighted to see how the paths they take to get there all have their own twists and turns. Rather than treading the exact same ground, each branch had me alternate between colosseum matches and more personal storylines. I’m happy I chose to play as Leda first, as her tale of vengeance was a wild ride to watch unfold. The story doesn’t shy away from how badly her desire for revenge affects those around her (which is spurred on by a cursed instrument she carries), and even though things never get as dark as they could have, she isn’t above gleefully describing to people how much they’d suffer if they got in her way.

I also came to admire how each of the paths in Fortune’s Weave are their own specific strands on a larger web of intrigue. It’s not exactly a new concept to have a secretive evil group pulling strings from the shadows, but it's the way each hero uncovers certain pieces of their motives and operations that compelled me the most. It never felt like I was stumbling through the dark trying to figure out what was going on, but more that each path provided new context to the events that were unfolding, which then leads to a dramatic twist in act two that was quite effective.

When stacked against these champions and their quests, my own character (who defaults to the name Eshmel) came off a little lackluster at first… but oddly enough, I didn’t really mind that. Compared to Byleth from Three Houses, who constantly fought for my attention between the other main characters, Fortune’s Weave is wise to put Eshmel in the background for the first half of the story while the others establish themselves, only swooping in at critical moments with their best Tuxedo Mask impression to ensure the heroes survive until the present day. Otherwise, Eshmel is content to chill out in town disguised in the form of a cute, plump little bird that everyone seems to love. In the final act, they take on a more commander-in-chief role, and though they end up sharing a lot of moments with the goddess helping you achieve your goals, their main role is support – and it’s something they do very well, bolstering your chosen squad with their incredible powers.

While their smaller role is ultimately a smart choice, it is a shame that Eshmel is largely silent outside of a few specific sequences, mostly chiming in through inconsequential dialogue choices accompanied by a simple, non-verbal gesture. Given how good the voice acting is across the whole cast, I didn’t really feel like I gained anything from these attempts at roleplay (aside from occasionally having companions interact with me in bird form, and then trying to pick the appropriate bird-response so I could… observe them… you know what, never mind).

Still, the visuals have improved greatly overall, from fluid zoom-ins as characters clash to the briefly animated and expressive character portraits during dialogue. Even sprinting or warping around the major hub city loads way faster than Garreg Mach Monastery in Three Houses. I still wish some scenes that weren’t cinematics had a bit of their own flair – I can only watch the screen fade to black and then have a single slice effect cut through it to signify someone did something with a weapon so many times. Thankfully, there are plenty of entertaining cutscenes saved for the bigger moments.

The meat of any Fire Emblem game is its tactical turn-based combat, and Fortune’s Weave does not disappoint on that front. Building off of Three Houses, the classic weapon triangle is replaced by other advantages and weaknesses ready to exploit on the battlefield. Little touches, like lances dealing more damage to cavalry or fist weapons making units more evasive, are just the tip of a strategic iceberg that got me to think differently. As my army clashed and my units increased in power, so too did their repertoire of combat arts and skills, adding increased power, evasion, or even the ability to stun and confuse opponents at the cost of a weapon’s durability.

One of the best additions to this battle math takes the form of incredibly rare swords that can cleave through undead enemies that would otherwise receive reduced damage from most sources. As I started to encounter more and more of the undead, figuring out who to bestow these weapons upon and where to deploy them became critical to my survival. At one point, I had a small squad fending off attacks from all sides, with their lone magical blade trading hands from one fighter to the next each turn so everyone had a fighting chance. Managing them is a cool wrinkle to consider that’s also full of thematic flavor.

Plenty of the main missions throw increasingly nasty curveballs at you.

Even though most battle maps have fairly standard objectives – take out leaders, rout the entire enemy force, etc. – plenty of the main missions throw some increasingly nasty curveballs at you. They continually forced me to adapt my tactics on the fly, reform my lines to deal with unexpected threats, and keep my team mobile to avoid new hazards and obstacles that appear all over the place. Rarely could I be complacent enough to slowly move across the map and let the enemy army slam into me bit by bit. Instead, I had to juggle split up squads, make risky strikes into well-defended territory, and ensure no one got left behind in the process.

My favorite addition by far is the introduction of a handful of cursed artifacts and the Blaze Arts they bestow upon many of the main characters. Their inclusion not only changed how I approached every battle, but made each of the four story paths even more unique. These cursed objects can let Cai launch a flame blast to hit several units, or let Dietrich teleport through barriers to close the distance on foes who thought themselves safe. I was very glad to have Leda on my first playthrough, as her ability to play a cursed instrument can buff a large number of allies at once, and her repertoire eventually expands to a song that gives everyone the ability to negate that undead defense bonus that had given me so much trouble.

There’s a clever and ever-building risk/reward system tied to these artifacts, as using Blaze Arts costs a bit of HP, which could easily leave my heroes exposed to a killing blow. These arts (along with using other cursed weapons and artifacts) increases a blaze gauge that boosts a unit’s stats when filled halfway… but reduces their maximum HP for the rest of the battle if the gauge fills completely. As the story continues to expand, so too do the opportunities to use these arts in some really exciting and strategic ways that I did not expect, making it more and more tempting to put lives on the line to ensure my team’s overall survival.

While Fortune’s Weave starts off fairly tame, the difficulty ramps up by the end of its first act, which took me about 50 hours to finish. Foes start to appear with better weapons than I could muster, promoted to even more advanced classes. By its much more condensed second act, I was running into all sorts of trouble, forcing me to turn to the gods for help. Expanding on a time rewinding feature first introduced in Three Houses, you can now invoke a god’s blessing to try things differently if your units start to drop – but Fortune’s Weave has built upon this idea with the ability to earn blessings from multiple gods.

Aside from the time rewind function, blessings can only be used one per turn in exchange for finite resources. I was able to literally pray to the gods of RNG to grant my team temporary bonuses like increased hit chance, evasion, and damage absorption to survive until the next round. This is entirely optional, of course, but it’s not just some “easy mode” crutch meant to entirely negate the difficulty. You’ll need to be smart to equip the right blessings before each battle starts, and know when to spend your limited currency to avert an incoming disaster and snatch victory from the impending jaws of defeat.

Much of my time between battles was spent wandering the streets of the capital city of Dagsion, and while it’s not exactly crowded, it does have a fair amount of hustle and bustle. I could explore the temples of the gods, mingle with the other gladiatorial hopefuls to scout potential recruits, and partake in other activities like weapon skill training or sharing meals while waiting for the next main mission. Unlike Three Houses, your exploration isn’t limited to just a few free days per month – instead, each day was mine to do as I pleased, and the more my renown grew across the land, the more facilities I gained access to.

A sprawling map is laid out for you to explore like a grand board game.

Time won’t pass just by training your units or sitting in the bathhouse, however, for the open road is where adventure truly lies. A sprawling map of the continent is laid out for you to explore like a grand board game, and in it hides a surprisingly deep layer of strategy and time management as you uncover roads that lead to points of interest across every corner of the land. Those include spots to feast or forage for supplies, random bands of enemies to test your mettle against, towns to visit and trade with for valuable gear, and small dungeons to delve into teeming with riches and upgrades. Four steps across the map costs one turn (which translates to a fourth of a full day), and the more I uncovered, the more I realized how important planning out my travels were given the campaign’s limited timeframe.

With anywhere from a few weeks to over a month between rounds in the Heroic Games, it was a fun challenge to juggle uncovering spots on the map that led me toward sidequest markers with finding the right moment to make my way back to the capital in time for certain special events – like spectating other teams in the competition to gain skill experience. I soon found myself eagerly devising plans for each of my outings across the world, looking for ways I could knock out a few nearby quest markers as I uncovered a new region.

If that somehow wasn’t enough, each hero has unique exploration skills that fundamentally changed how I planned my expeditions. Theodora, for instance, is the only hero who can recruit battalions at towns and employ them in battle to unleash devastating area of effect attacks (something your enemies will start doing even if your chosen hero cannot), while only Cai can find spots to tame wild animals to serve as personalized rides for mounted units, giving them additional stat boosts the more they bond with their ride.

Since many of the activities both in the city and out in the world replenish each week, there was more motivation to bounce back and forth between the two and divide my time as best I could. That said, the allure of a giant, ever-expanding map often proved too enticing to ignore, and I happily allowed myself to be distracted from returning to “home base” in favor of uncovering new ground — especially with so many hidden dungeons to find.

Unlike the traditional top down skirmishes found elsewhere, dungeons build off of ideas first introduced way back in Shadows of Valentia for the 3DS. You pick a small group of five from your larger army when you enter one, and each is teeming with enemies you can either sneak and dash around or lunge toward to initiate combat. These clashes are more akin to a battle you’d see in a classic JRPG, with both teams forming a line and alternating attacks. Though it’s a fairly simplified system, there are short bursts of fun to be had here, almost like a minigame.

Just like in the larger battles, picking the right fighter to attack against an opposing unit that is poised to retaliate can be the difference between cleaving off a chunk of your team’s shared HP and negating their strike with the right foil. I’ll admit, early on it sometimes came down to just having a highly defensive tank in the party to soak all incoming blows – but as the difficulty ramped up, so too did the enemy variety. Thankfully, the ability to link up attacks or have one ally heal while another struck out meant my group could survive even longer in these dungeons, allowing me to find cool treasures like those cursed weapons.

It’s not truly a Fire Emblem game unless you’re slowly building an army out of a rag-tag crew of miscreants from all walks of life, and while Fortune’s Weave doesn’t break from that tradition entirely, it opts for a slightly different approach. By the time each of the four main heroes reaches the Heroic Games at Dagsion, they’ll have their own small crew of (mostly) trusted allies. But the colosseum fights are much bigger skirmishes, and you’ll need to bolster your ranks if you want to survive. As luck would have it, wandering the capital can feel a bit like window shopping for the deadliest mercenaries in the land.

I had to ensure I was properly scouting recruits and spending time with them.

Almost every potential recruit has their own conditions that need to be met before they’ll agree to join your group. Most will want you to have achieved a certain level of renown from questing, but you’ll have to build enough support so that they trust you as well, a process that involves things like taking them out for fine dining or to the theater. Some may even have a final negotiation to resolve, like handing over certain items or money (one character actually quizzed me on the region to see if I’d been paying attention in my exploration). Fortune’s Weave even cleverly mixes up these requirements depending on who you’re playing as, and some may not want to join certain characters at all, giving you an extra incentive to explore other story paths. This creates another fun wrinkle in the time management between missions, as I had to ensure I was properly scouting recruits who were the best fit for my team and allocating time to spend with them while in the capital (as well as finding gifts for them while traveling abroad).

I was unsure about this system at the start, especially what it meant for the overarching story. Picking up random mercenaries at unpredictable points means they don’t really add much to the main story (though you can still unlock your fair share of support conversations with them). Instead, each hero usually trades words with only the small group they form at the start of their story during important moments, which makes everyone else feel less important. However, I soon realized this approach works out for the better for a few reasons.

For one, it allows for a more intimate story to unfold, without having to worry about some random bandit I picked up chiming in with something thoughtful. The second reason I did not anticipate is that it makes room for your main gladiator “rivals” to shine. It’s not just the four champions you choose from that are in the running to be crowned winner of the Heroic Games, as you’ll soon spot other teams around the capital led by some pretty charismatic characters.

Much like how each story path touches on different aspects of the main antagonists, you’ll also have different interactions with the other team leaders. Early on, you’re even able to team up with some of them during qualifying rounds to get a taste of their power, and it turns out they’re just as capable as you. I really enjoyed getting to temporarily command leaders like the laser gun-toting Anatolia (no, I will not elaborate) or the mask-wearing priestess Orchel, as they had their own unique spin on Blaze Arts that differed greatly from any of the main heroes. (My only slight disappointment stemmed from getting spoiled on one character’s mysterious backstory by… their own info page, which described their true nature while they were a guest in my party, before it was formally revealed.)

These rivals become more formidable when it's your turn to face off against them, and depending on which story path you’re on, it’s even possible to help them out with special missions after they drop out of the Heroic Games. These “paralogues” might be low in quantity, but they were all extremely fun and challenging. My favorite included helping one character escort civilians out of a map dominated by a giant beast summoning tentacles all over the place – getting everyone out alive forced me to be extremely precise, stunning the ridiculously powerful creature at just the right moments while I made a break for the exit. Completing these paralogues also had some pretty great and far-reaching effects on the story at large, which once again made the idea of going back to see the ones on another path all the more enticing.

With so much to consider and plan around outside of combat, it’s easy to get overwhelmed and lose sight of your immediate objectives. At one point, I felt myself starting to get torn as I tried to do everything at once, which is when the true appeal of Fortune’s Weave became clear to me. It’s better to think of its story not as a five-course meal you need to march through as you try and finish everything, but rather as an all-you-can-eat buffet. You’re not expected to eat the entire buffet!

The paralogues have some pretty great and far-reaching effects on the story.

Instead, I focused on exactly what I wanted: recruiting a handful of characters that caught my eye, doing weapon training whenever I happened to be back in town to promote my units to better classes, maybe giving away a few gifts, and trying to complete a few quests out in the world before coming back to town. Anyone I didn’t end up recruiting would still be there for another story path, and the same was true of any dungeons I didn’t uncover or the far reaches of the map I didn’t have time to travel to. I was always allowed to be as comprehensive or as relaxed as I wanted to be. Sure, exploring a mine could mean I find materials to refine or repair weapons to use more combat arts, but I could also just use those arts more sparingly, and then spend that time leveling my units until the next mission to compensate.

Fortune’s Weave even extends that freedom of choice to its second act in a pretty wild way, though I’ll avoid specific spoilers. As the story escalates, whichever hero you’ve progressed with most is drawn into a string of intimidating, large-scale battles where the calendar and exploration elements are removed. It’s a much more condensed arc, and its battles become incredibly grueling across maps that are much larger than those in the first act. What surprised me is that entering this second part of the story informed me that I could opt to , which would then auto-level my units appropriately for act three and provide a TL:DR version of how the story advanced.

Along with being able to replay these missions whenever I wanted, the ability to skip them outright is a pretty thoughtful one for subsequent playthroughs using different heroes… but I was a little shocked it gave me this option on my first run. I, of course, declined this offer, and was much happier flexing my strategic muscles on these satisfyingly tough battles (though that happiness turned to outright horror around the time I found myself staring down four giant war elephants on a bridge, all charging in my direction).

All of this leads to Fortune’s Weave’s final act, and while I still won’t delve into plot details, it’s worth touching lightly on just how insane things get. It took me around 70 hours to reach this point, and the momentum could have easily become a slow shamble to the finish line as it retreads familiar ground. And yet, it wasn’t until this point – when all of the individual stories merged into one – that Fortune’s Weave evolved from a great adventure into a truly phenomenal RPG.

The way its grand world map is recontextualized from something I had spent countless hours exploring into a centerpiece for tactical warfare gave me an immense thrill. This section had smart answers ready for how I could best make use of an army that had grown awfully crowded (regardless of how many or how few individual story paths I had completed by that point). It introduces not only great new methods to manage those troops, but does so in a way where nobody was truly left without a purpose, and it encouraged as much multi-tasking as I wanted to delve into (and man did I ever delve). In nearly every respect, it was the perfect culmination of strategy and management that I had been honing over the course of this story, providing just as many challenges as new tools to overcome them. Even Eshmel finally gets their chance to shine, using their otherworldly power to lead the charge.

Truthfully, I probably spent way more time than needed doing everything I could before the final showdown, but I never once felt compelled to simply run down the clock. There were so many ways I wanted to optimize my forces, and even then my adversaries were definitely not taking it easy on me. These final missions tested the limit of my ability to see all my allies safely through to the end thanks to some downright devious battlefields filled with punishing traps, and I wouldn’t have a high-stakes conclusion be any other way.

items.title: Trails In The Sky 2nd Chapter Review
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
One of the biggest hurdles of the Trails series was how to introduce its world to new players when almost every game is interconnected through multiple follow-up entries. After all, the original The Legend of Heroes: Trails in the Sky subseries was only on PC and older handhelds like the PSP. Fortunately, developer Falcom remedied that with the excellent Trails in the Sky 1st Chapter remake last year – finally, an approachable way to start where the trail began with a slick 3D makeover and updated gameplay. Swiftly following up with a remake of Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter, this RPG retains all of the best qualities of the original version, such as its story, side quests, and characters, while simultaneously giving it that visual and gameplay overhaul to fit modern standards.

Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter picks up right where its predecessor ends with our bubbly and confident heroine, Estelle Bright. Now that her adoptive brother and best friend Joshua Bright suddenly recalled his true origins and has disappeared, Estelle is dead set on finding him and bringing him home. It also digs deeper and fleshes out the cultish revelations that were unearthed towards the end of 1st Chapter. As a result, it gives 2nd Chapter heavier stakes from onset, but also with the emotionally resonant edge that keeps you invested.

The characters are equally zany too, and they’re brimming with personality. Estelle’s, ahem, , demeanor contrasts nicely with Joshua’s now brooding mood. The two theater nerds in Olivier and the villainous Blueblanc face off in a duel of overindulgent poetry to see who can out-cringe each other. It’s all entertaining to watch and the experience is bolstered thanks to the addition of full voice acting (whereas the original Trails in the Sky games only had voice acting for the combat). In these Sky remakes, the script and story are brought to life even more so with those original voice actors of Estelle and Joshua reprising their roles. It feels like a full-circle moment, especially for fans who’ve stuck with Trails since the beginning.

2nd Chapter is virtually a faithful 1:1 recreation of the original in terms of story structure and side quests, so you’ll be running around Liberl Kingdom going through the same cities and locations as you did in 1st Chapter. While that might seem like a rehash, the order in which you visit them in this sequel is rearranged. Along with a completely different slate of side quests to tackle from the previous adventure, it makes this journey feel much less like a retread and more like revisiting an old home.

There aren’t any multiple divergent storylines that cross together with later entries like Trails and , which also came with a roguelite dungeon where all the characters could interact outside of the story. It works in 2nd Chapter’s favor as it isn’t unnecessarily bogged down with extra story content simply for the sake of having something new. It’s a streamlined adventure that’s easy to follow without superfluous bloat that some later Trails entries would suffer from.

It isn’t bogged down with superfluous bloat simply to have something new.

That being said, the pacing in the last chapter before heading into the finale is a bit stunted since you're required to backtrack through previous locations one final time due to story reasons. The issue is that almost all of your fast travel points that you unlocked before disappear, and you’ll have to activate them again, which makes this particular bump in the road a slog.

Leaning into a stylized anime-inspired art direction with these remakes brings bolder colors and a new vision for familiar worlds, however. The transition between combat phases are smoother, and the use of more camera angles and sharp cuts give attacks and crafts more cinematic flair. You can see close ups of every character’s fierce facial expressions as they shout out and execute their attacks in ways that you never could with the top-down sprites of the original. The new character models and animations give the story some extra life, whether it’s the party enjoying themselves while exploring the world or fighting for their lives against an all-powerful foe.

The character animations look a lot less awkward in both gameplay and cutscenes, and in critical junctures, they do a lot to add weight for its more serious, pivotal moments. Along with that, the political machinations and turmoil that dictate its world, and the origins of what you see further in the series, feel more fully realized. And the story here in Sky 2nd Chapter strikes a wonderful momentum for concluding Estelle's and Joshua’s character arcs cleanly and concisely without prolonging them – it’s something that other protagonists suffered a bit from in later Trails sagas.

This remake benefits from 13 games and over 20 years of iterations, taking the framework of existing gameplay systems from Trails games that came before. While the original version was purely turn-based, 2nd Chapter quite heavily borrows the real-time and turn-based hybrid system that the entries started. You can attack enemies in-real time in the field (Quick Battles) to whittle them down and stun them to gain an advantage, then immediately transition to the main turn-based combat (Command Battles). Some Trails purists may not like the change to hybrid combat, but it’s the biggest change that makes it stand out from the original.

A significant difference in the Sky remakes is the addition of Brave Points (BP), which were introduced in the Cold Steel saga – you accumulate them by landing critical hits, stunning enemies, or hitting stunned enemies. Depending on how many BP you spend, you can initiate Brave Attacks which include follow-up hits from an ally, coordinated chain strikes, or an all-out group burst like that in Persona for additional damage. It makes 2nd Chapter’s combat much more engaging and explosive than the original’s.

2nd Chapter also cleverly merges and evolves the hybrid and BP mechanics together. In the Daybreak games, Van and his crew would just to deal extra damage if a Command battle started with an advantage. However, when you enter them with an advantage in Sky 2nd Chapter, you can launch a preemptive Brave Attack, letting you start off the fight with a powerful Brave Chain or Burst move. It’s impressive that 2nd Chapter doesn’t merely just copy and paste combat mechanics from previous Trails entries, but further refines them into something more satisfying.

BP can also be consumed during Quick battles in the form of a Brave Rush, which are powerful hits that deal exceedingly more stun damage, allowing you to enter into an advantage state faster. It’s helpful on larger enemies who are more resilient to stun, but there’s a strategic trade off. Since Brave Rush uses BP, you’ll enter the Command phase with fewer BP, meaning you might not have enough to initiate a preemptive Brave Attack. Give-and-take compromises like these ensure that the battle system remains relatively balanced and challenging.

Brave Rushes weren’t in Daybreak’s hybrid battles, and so the Sky remakes have a dedicated button for it. While it’s a welcome addition to the combat, it’s actually also the tipping point that makes the control scheme for Quick battles a bit unwieldy. In particular, all modern Trails games have a high-speed mode, which as its name suggests, accelerates overall game speed at any time. In previous games, this was a simple one-button toggle on the controller, but in these remakes, you have to press the left and right bumpers at the same time to toggle it. As a longtime Trails player, I’ve been conditioned to the one-button toggle for high-speed mode so it's a bit of an annoying change, but it’s a very miniscule problem in the grand scheme of things.

Sky 2nd Chapter further refines combat mechanics into something more satisfying.

As with all other Trails games, the timeline mechanic makes its welcome return once again, clearly showing the turn order of allies and enemies. Randomized turn bonuses continue to add variability, augmenting the abilities of whomever’s turn icon is lined up with it, whether friend or foe. These can range from automatic HP recovery, guaranteed critical hits, to eliminating both casting time and cost (called Zero Arts). Sure, beating enemies is gratifying, but much of that feeling comes from manipulating the timeline order through different spells and special attacks (called Crafts) while making the most of their innate effects.

Is there a critical hit icon next to a monster casting a spell? Agate’s Draguna Blast can inflict Impede to interrupt spellcasting. The enemy will still be able to land a critical hit with whatever their next non-casting attack will be, but at least they won’t be able to fire off that devastating spell. You’ve postponed the inevitable, giving you a moment of reprieve in this volatile yet orderly battle system. But what if you don’t want to leave it to chance, you can use Zin’s True Heralding Fist to inflict Delay, which pushes down bonuses farther down the timeline so that it’ll land on someone else, preferably one of your allies. It’s instances like these where you have to balance dishing out as much damage as possible with managing the combat timeline for bonuses that could change the tide of battle.

Despite making it easier to steal bonuses compared to its predecessor, the Sky remakes simplify it further. For example, certain offensive Crafts like Estelle’s Comet have a “Steal Bonus” effect, which lets her do just that. While not every character has a regular Craft with that effect, all offensive S-Crafts (ultimate attacks) do, giving every character the ability to steal bonuses in some capacity. It’s a really useful change because it synergizes well with the fact that you can now stack multiple bonuses onto one character. You can have HP recovery, critical hit, and Zero Arts icons activate all in one turn if you play your cards right. Playing around with delay and stealing effects adds a fun twist, with trade-off being your house of cards potentially collapsing because enemies can also steal bonuses and undo all your hard work. Don’t get too greedy!

2nd Chapter uses Daybreak’s free roam during Command battles, so your team is able to move as much as they want around the battlefield without using up a turn. It’s crucial to position your characters properly because now everyone’s Crafts have been updated with new effects, including the aforementioned Steal Bonus effect. For example, Kloe’s Kämpfer in the original game only lowered enemies’ strength and defense stats, but in this remake, it now also does extra damage when striking an enemy from the side as opposed to the front or back. It’s small changes like these that help 2nd Chapter feel modern and up to date with recent Trails entries.

The Orbment system continues to be a great way to customize magic spells and perks for each character. These remakes surprisingly mirror the original’s system as it doesn’t have Cold Steel's broken buildcrafting or Daybreak’s multitude of passive Shard abilities. Here, where you place your elemental gems (called Quartz) determines which spells a certain character can use. Whereas in Daybreak everyone had the same four different lines in their Orbments to slot Quartz in, 2nd Chapter’s set up is more rigid

Magically-oriented characters can have their Quartz setup to unlock higher tier spells, as opposed to those who are physical-focused. This stricter system reflects a much more old-school RPG approach as if to have specialized character classes. It’s more straightforward to understand, and initially feels a little underdeveloped coming from the openness and flexibility of Orbment systems in other Trails entries. But in a field of revisions, it’s admirable to at least see one aspect of gameplay in these Sky remakes that staunchly sticks to its roots.

items.title: Golden Axe Animated Series Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
It’s understandable to feel somewhat cynical and pre-exhausted about Golden Axe going into it, simply because the entire approach of a snarky, self-aware animated series is, generally speaking, very well worn territory at this point and can feel like something of a safety net rather than trying for a more straightforward and earnest approach. Then there’s also the fact that joke-driven fantasy stories in particular are also quite familiar terrain both in and out of animation, encompassing everything from The Princess Bride to Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves.

Having seen the entire first season, I can say that Golden Axe is certainly doing what you’d expect, as it takes the characters and concepts from the and its sequels and remixes them into a decidedly wacky, high energy cartoon. But after some initial bumps in the road, the series gradually grew on me through its ten episodes thanks to some solid laughs, great voice acting, and its overall good nature.

Obviously adapting any familiar IP is tricky territory, as fans can be just abit possessive and sensitive about how a beloved pre-existing universe is handled — just ask Zach Cregger — but Golden Axe feels like a safer title than some for going this route. Its heyday was in the arcade era, its most recent installment was a poorly received 2008 game, and it never had the deepest or most complex mythology. Of course, you’ll still find many angry comments below Golden Axe’s trailer saying that they’re upset that this is a comedic take on the serious property they remember. I get it, but also… it’s Golden Axe, guys! It’s a genuinely fun game, but as someone who’s old enough to have fond memories of playing the original in arcades, it’s also not a title we need to be precious about, especially given that this show never feels spiteful about its source material.

The game’s original heroic trio of Ax Battler, Tyris Flare, and Gilius Thunderhead all play large roles here, but the story kicks off with Gilius having a spat with the others that leads to him splitting off from them on a parallel quest through the land of Yuria alongside an overeager protogree named Hampton Squib, who’s the main new addition to the canon in this series. Meanwhile, Ax and Tyris replace Gilius with Chronos, a character culled from , while all the characters simultaneously hope to take down the villainous Death Adder, who has control of the powerful weapon known as the Golden Axe.

If there’s a lead character in this ensemble, it’s definitely Gilius the battle dwarf, voiced here by the always excellent Matthew Rhys, currently riding high on much deserved adoration for Widow’s Bay. Rhys is incredibly fun playing the crusty and stubborn Gilius, going big when the scene calls for it in all the right ways. If you’ve enjoyed hearing him yell out in terror on Widow’s Bay, you’ll also enjoy some of Rhys’ reactions here, including an especially prolonged scream at one point.

Voicing Hampton, Danny Pudi makes for a perfect partner for Rhys, bringing just the right kind of youthful, optimistic energy the character calls for (it doesn’t matter that Pudi’s pushing 50 in real life; this is a cartoon!). And Liam McIntyre, Lisa Gilroy, and Carl Tart all know exactly the kind of humorously self-confident vibes with which to imbue their characters, voicing Ax, Tyris, and Chronos respectively.

Still, with the show keeping our heroes in two distinct groups for so much of the season, there’s stronger material for the Gilius and Hampton portions overall, with the dimwitted Ax and the arrogant Tyris sometimes providing too similar of a feel with their single-minded, overconfident approach. Chronos the cat man — or panther man if you ask him — at least provides a different, more offbeat energy.

The tone and sense of humor of Golden Axe evokes the likes of Rick and Morty and Star Trek: Lower Decks, and also replicates the strengths and weaknesses of those series and others like them. This isn’t a shock, given that Golden Axe has writers who worked on Rick and Morty, and that one of the two creators — Mike McMahan, teamed here with Joe Chandler — was in fact the creator of Lower Decks as well.

Like those series, Golden Axe is rapid fire with its jokes, with mixed results. There are some duds to be sure, and some gags are way too telegraphed or obvious, but there are also many really strong and even outright hysterical moments as well as we watch these guys and their enemies hack and slash their way across the land, mega-gore included. One particularly strong ongoing element is how the series uses the game’s skeleton warriors, who get to represent all sorts of different mundane personality types as we see them make small talk, bully one another, or complain when they can’t hear their boss’ big speech.

Shades of Lower Decks and Rick and Morty, Golden Axe can be aat times, feeling overly frenetic and sometimes outright abrasive with its in-your-face approach. But after the early episodes lean dangerously far in this direction, the pacing improves as the season continues, and the characters become better defined and more likable, including the addition of a notably upbeat skeleton voiced by the always welcome presence of Stephanie Beatriz.

The show rarely breaks the fourth wall outright — though the funny offscreen narrator, voiced by SungWon Cho, certainly pushes things further — but continually takes a winking approach to both video game tropes in general and to elements of Golden Axe specifically. Yes, the wonderfully ridiculous name Ax Battler, and the fact that the dude uses a sword and not an axe, is addressed in a scene that is both amusing yet also certainly low-hanging fruit.

It’s comedically deconstructing the familiar aspects of the IP with which it’s working, but from the perspective of someone who definitely understands and knows the original well.

I particularly loved how the show incorporates the magic potions from the game, and the bizarre manner in which you’d replenish those potions by literally kicking small little creatures known as Thieves. The show’s exploration of what exactly the deal is with one of these Thieves, his home life included, is one of the season’s highlights. Also a standout is the fifth episode of the season, which comes up with a plot device to directly recreate the game’s imagery in an entertaining manner.

The self-parody and winking approach feels like it’s done with affection in Golden Axe. As with Lower Decks, it’s comedically deconstructing the familiar aspects of the IP with which it’s working, but from the perspective of someone who definitely understands and knows the original well. It doesn’t come across as either mockery or self-loathing, because yes, the beast from the games known as Chicken Leg is in this show, and yes, he’s very silly but he’s also very lovable.

items.title: Forgotten Island Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
Having already made a standout film for DreamWorks Animation with 2022’s Puss in Boots: The Last Wish, directors Joel Crawford and Januel Mercado have reteamed for the wonderful Forgotten Island, which manages to tell a story that’s both deeply personal and impressively fantastical in equal measure.

Also written by Crawford and Mercado, Forgotten Island centers on recent high school graduates Jo and Raissa (voiced, respectively, by the winning pairing of singer-songwriter H.E.R. and Liza Soberano), whose longtime friendship is about to be tested in a big way, as Raissa prepares to move from the Philippines to America in order to attend Caltech. The night before Raissa is to leave, the two find themselves transported to Nakali, a mystical world filled with creatures from Filipino folklore just like Jo’s late grandmother, Lola Fatima (Dolly de Leon), had told them about. Now they must find their way back home while also trying to figure out what exactly happened in a 12-hour gap in their memories that’s obscuring what exactly occurred after they first arrived in this strange land.

Forgotten Island is skillfully told and easy to connect with from the start, well before any fantasy elements are introduced. Vaguely set in the late ’80s-early ’90s (based on the technology and music), the film quickly cements Jo and Raissa as an especially lovable comedic duo, starting with showing how they came to be best friends as kids. While Jo is the more overt wild child and Raissa the scientifically adept nerdy one, the two bond over a mutual love of the weird and the macabre — and sometimes, a love for putting themselves in dangerous scenarios — in a very funny series of scenes that shows their adoration of all things strange and offbeat. This includes stories involving the creatures Lola Fatima tells them about, which they eagerly recreate onstage for their classmates, "splash zone” included thanks to the copious amounts of fake blood with which they splatter the crowd.

Though the movie is certainly accessible for younger kids, filled with clever gags that can be appreciated regardless of age, Crawford and Mercado are aware that some kids share a love for fun and freaky stuff from an early age, infusing Jo and Raissa with a huge sense of relatable joy for those who share their specific tastes. Beyond that, and most importantly, it’s easy to believe in and connect to their deep bond and the sense of finding your kindred spirit as a kid, regardless of what your specific shared interests are.

As for the Forgotten Island of the title, Nakali is filled with a bevy of fantastic creatures of all shapes and sizes, starting with Raww (an exuberant Dave Franco), a weredog who guides our heroes on their journey, having spent those missing 12 hours partying with them. Then you have the baby-like Bungi (Manny Jacinto); the memory-collecting Batiba (Jenny Slate); the aquatic Mermahn (Kevin McCann); and the diminutive King Truffle Wuffle (Ronny Chieng), whose angry, combative nature is undercut by an innate physical adorableness he despises. All of these characters play notable roles along the way, while Jo and Raissa also come into conflict with the Manang (Lea Salonga), a ferocious, fanged, clawed creature called a Manananggal, whose abilities include bisecting herself at the waist into two halves when needed.

As you might glean by that description above, Manang is a genuinely unsettling presence, vividly depicted by the film’s excellent animation. As proven by the character Death in Puss in Boots: The Last Wish, Crawford and Mercado are willing to go further than your typical family animated movie when it comes to making their villains truly feel ominous and menacing, and Manang definitely reinforces this in a highly effective manner. Part of Raissa and Jo’s memory gap has Raissa waking up with Manang’s wings somehow now on her back and attached by two demonic-looking hands that hold onto her shoulders, which is one of many cool and creepy touches in the film before we even see Manang herself hunting her prey.

Forgotten Island juggles its many elements incredibly well, with moments that evoke the likes of Scott Pilgrim vs. The World in terms of the film’s style and energy, intermixed with a ton of legitimately funny comedy bits coexisting alongside its awesome looking and fascinating creatures. Its depiction of Filipino culture, both via Jo and Raissa’s everyday life and through the folklore explored, is also wonderfully interwoven into the film’s fabric, providing a vivid, welcoming window whether you're familiar with any of it beforehand or not.

It’s a great movie about the power of the history of friendship and the significance of the shared memories we make with the people we love. 

But at the heart of the film is Jo and Raissa’s friendship, and yeah, you could snark about how this is another movie about “the power of friendship,” which it absolutely is, but it’s a movie about the power of friendship. It’s also a great movie about the power of the of friendship and the significance of the shared memories we make with the people we love.

Raissa and Jo’s missing 12 hours are a strong comedy engine, making this sort of a family friendly version of The Hangover as they awaken to many signs — from odd new clothing they’re wearing to Raissa’s half-shaved head (and her new wings!) to the crude new matching tattoos Jo and Raww have — that some truly wild shenanigans went down the night before. But they’re also setting up integral aspects of the film as it continues, and our two heroes have to make some big decisions about just how important memories can be in relation to who we are today.

items.title: The Creep Tapes Season 3 Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
The Creep Tapes: Season 3 debuts September 15 on Shudder and AMC+ with the first two episodes of the 6-episode season.

It’s no easy feat keeping a series interesting once it hits its middle years, especially those with a formula or structure crucial to its core. Thankfully for Patrick Brice and Mark Duplass, the third season of their television brainchild, , shows no signs of slowing down on that front, much like high-concept cousins 24 and Lost in their time. While it’s far from the same kind of show in story and plot, the Shudder horror series is like-minded in its dedication to encouraging its concept to go as far as it needs to go. That mindset is crucial in making these kinds of shows work, and The Creep Tapes continues to prove what a winning concept centering the show on a serial killer known as Peachfuzz (or Josef, or…) and his world has been from day one.

As the show has proven in its desire to explore and play within the found footage structure — and, as a result, to push it to places we haven’t seen it go before — since the first season, that continuing desire has become a necessary foundation in keeping the audience invested in Peachfuzz’s twisted story. In Season 3, that spirited sense of experimentation still permeates the entire project in a way that feels fresh and inspired.

It’s no easy feat keeping a series interesting once it hits its middle years, but the third season of The Creep Tapes shows no signs of slowing down.

The found footage conundrum, where filmmakers sometimes struggle to build stories that don’t feel laden with overdone tropes of the subgenre, is almost nowhere to be found in the show’s latest batch of tapes. Sure, the series still sometimes relies on the basic premise that got it here in the first place, and employs classic found footage tropes that are staples of the medium — even rendering the episodes a tad slow here and there — but it almost always ups the ante in the next moment. In fact, this season reaches some serious heights with a top-notch episode that takes place on a private plane… and that’s all I’m giving you, because I refuse to spoil an excellent episode that you should see for yourself. It’s once again clear that Brice and Duplass aren’t messing around when it comes to crafting killer compact narratives that service the greater story.

Speaking of story, the films that started the Creep Tapes saga — 2014’s Creep, starring Duplass and Brice; and 2017’s Creep 2, with Duplass and the smart and fierce Desiree Akhavan — laid pretty basic but wonderful groundwork for a tale that could’ve stayed simple. The movies packed a punch with the basic premise, but then The Creep Tapes went back over previously tread ground and tilled the soil again, allowing its audience to discover what was buried beneath. Season 3 is no exception, and though we’re still discovering pieces to the puzzle, it feels very satisfying to see new bread crumbs being laid in the wonderful cosmic trenches that are Peachfuzz’s secretive origins and upbringing.

Another element of the series that continues to keep us hungry for more Creep is Duplass himself. He’s been playing this character for over a decade now, and it so easily could’ve lost its spark for him somewhere along the way, especially with the found footage conceit, which can be limiting to those unwilling or unable to think outside the box. Instead, Peachfuzz has only become more intriguing and enticing to the man who embodies him, and boy does it show in the work. Duplass is just as smug, beguiling, unsettling, and downright insane as ever in Season 3, and he reminds the audience once again that this character is one that deserves a permanent spot in the horror hall of fame.

As always, Duplass and his monumental character would be incomplete, and far less interesting to watch, without a cast of victims as well crafted as he is. All of Peachfuzz’s prey thus far bring a sense of sobering humanity (and various degrees of hilarity) to the terrifying, unfortunate, and almost absurd situation of being stuck in the same place as our central antagonist. It’s both a writing and a performance thing, and this season’s crop of guest stars is as good as ever.
